to come, go

Of this verb, Aeschylus uses, besides the present, the perfect ἐλήλυθα, the aorist ἦλθον (with dual ἠλθέτην Ag. 1207, as Elmsley correctly wrote for ἤλθετον) and the remaining moods ἐλθέ, ἔλθοιμι, ἔλθω, ἐλθεῖν, ἐλθών, the future ἐλεύσομαι (for which the Attics prefer to say εἶμι) in only two places, Pr. 854, Suppl. 522, as Sophocles OC. 1206, Tr. 595. I come, I approach, I go. It is said either of people who come somewhere or of things that befall someone.
In the proper meaning of coming, without a case.
With the dative of the person to whom something happens.
